questions.q: SDG 7 focuses on 'Affordable and Clean Energy.' Which architectural strategy involves using a building's design—rather than mechanical systems—to maintain comfortable temperatures?
questions.n: Passive design uses the building's orientation, thermal mass, and natural ventilation to regulate temperature without external energy input.

questions.q: Under SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), what is the term for a material that can 'sense' environmental changes and respond to them, such as photochromic glass?
questions.n: Smart materials have one or more properties that can be significantly changed in a controlled fashion by external stimuli.

questions.q: SDG 15 focuses on 'Life on Land.' In urban planning, what is the term for a network of natural and semi-natural areas designed to deliver a wide range of ecosystem services?
questions.n: Green infrastructure uses natural systems (like wetlands and parks) to manage water, reduce heat, and provide habitats.

questions.q: SDG 6 targets 'Clean Water and Sanitation.' Which system collects and treats wastewater from sinks and showers for reuse in flushing toilets or irrigation?
questions.n: Greywater is wastewater from non-toilet plumbing fixtures and is relatively easy to treat for secondary non-potable uses.

questions.q: SDG 13 concerns 'Climate Action.' What is the architectural term for the total amount of greenhouse gas emissions associated with the entire life cycle of a building material?
questions.n: Embodied carbon accounts for the emissions from mining, manufacturing, transporting, and installing materials.

questions.q: SDG 11 includes the protection of cultural and natural heritage. What is the process of changing an old building for a purpose other than which it was originally designed?
questions.n: This strategy breathes new life into old structures, such as turning an old warehouse into loft apartments.

questions.q: In line with SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption), what design philosophy advocates for products and buildings to be designed with their end-of-life in mind?
questions.n: This biomimetic approach models human industry on nature's processes, where materials are viewed as nutrients circulating in healthy loops.

questions.q: SDG 11.7 aims to provide universal access to safe, inclusive, and accessible green and public spaces. Which design strategy uses plants on building roofs to reduce the 'Urban Heat Island' effect?
questions.n: Vegetated roof covers help cool buildings and their surroundings through evapotranspiration and shading.

questions.q: SDG 3 promotes 'Good Health and Well-being.' Which design concept focuses on increasing occupant connectivity to the natural environment through the use of direct nature, indirect nature, and space/place conditions?
questions.n: Biophilic design seeks to satisfy the inherent human need to affiliate with nature in the built environment.

questions.q: SDG 9 encourages 'Resilient Infrastructure.' In earthquake-prone regions, what technology allows a building to move independently from the ground to prevent structural failure?
questions.n: Base isolators act like shock absorbers between the foundation and the structure, decoupling it from ground motion.

questions.q: Which specific SDG 6 target is addressed by the architectural implementation of an on-site 'DEWATS' (Decentralized Wastewater Treatment System)?
o: Improving water quality by reducing pollution and halving the proportion of untreated wastewater
Expanding international cooperation in water harvesting
Universal access to safe drinking water
questions.n: DEWATS allows buildings to treat waste locally rather than discharging raw sewage into municipal lines or natural bodies of water.

questions.q: In the context of SDG 7, what is the primary difference between a 'BIPV' system and a standard rooftop solar array?
o: Standard solar arrays cannot be connected to the municipal grid.
BIPV serves as both the outer skin of the building and an energy generator.
BIPV systems only work during cloudy weather.
BIPV is significantly cheaper than standard solar panels.
questions.n: Building Integrated Photovoltaics replace conventional materials like glass or shingles, performing a dual structural and functional role.

questions.q: Regarding SDG 12, what is the core requirement for a building material to be certified as 'Cradle-to-Cradle' (C2C) rather than 'Cradle-to-Grave'?
o: It must be made of at least 50% recycled content.
It must be biodegradable or infinitely recyclable into the same quality of material.
The material must be carbon-neutral during the manufacturing phase.
It must be sourced within a 500-mile radius of the construction site.
questions.n: C2C creates a closed-loop system where waste becomes 'food' for a new product, preventing downcycling or landfilling.

questions.q: Under Universal Design Principle 4 (Perceptible Information), which feature would be essential for a building's emergency egress system?
o: Eliminating all steps and level changes
Redundant cueing using both visual and audible alarms
A door that opens automatically with a sensor
A wider door leaf to accommodate wheelchairs
questions.n: Perceptible information requires that critical data is communicated effectively regardless of a user's sensory abilities.

questions.q: Which 'Smart Material' technology contributes to SDG 11 by reducing the energy required for cooling through its ability to change transparency based on heat?
questions.n: Thermochromic materials react to temperature changes, tinting automatically to block solar heat gain when the sun is at its peak.

questions.q: In the pursuit of SDG 15 (Life on Land), an architect uses 'Xeriscaping' for a project. What is the primary characteristic of this technique?
o: The use of elaborate water fountains to cool the air
The removal of all vegetation to prevent wildfires
Landscaping that requires little to no supplemental water from irrigation
Growing food vertically on the facade of the building
questions.n: By using native, drought-tolerant plants, xeriscaping preserves local water resources and supports local biodiversity.

questions.q: Which principle of Universal Design is violated if an accessible entrance is located at the back of the building while the main entrance has stairs?
questions.n: Equitable use requires that the design is marketable to all and avoids segregating or stigmatizing any users.

questions.q: As part of SDG 13 (Climate Action), an architect calculates the 'Albedo' of a roofing material. What does a high Albedo signify?
o: The material has a very high embodied carbon content.
The material is highly porous and allows for water drainage.
The material reflects a high proportion of sunlight, keeping the building cooler.
The material absorbs a high amount of solar radiation.
questions.n: Materials with high albedo (like white roofs) reflect energy back into space, reducing the need for air conditioning.

questions.q: Which component of an 'Aquaponics' system (SDG 2) is responsible for converting toxic ammonia into nitrates that plants can absorb?
questions.n: Bacteria living in the system act as the biological filter, performing the chemical conversion necessary for the plants to grow.

questions.q: Universal Design Principle 5, 'Tolerance for Error,' is best exemplified by which of the following architectural features?
o: A 'Fail-Safe' feature on an elevator that prevents it from moving if the door is obstructed
Providing clear floor space for a wheelchair turning radius
Using icons instead of text on restroom signs
Using a high-contrast color scheme for stairs
questions.n: This principle focuses on minimizing hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions.

questions.q: An architect is designing a library. To adhere to SDG 10 and the principle of 'Equitable Use,' how should the checkout counters be designed?
o: Installing a high counter only, but providing a bell to call for assistance
Designing a single, continuous counter height that is accessible to both standing and seated users
Providing a separate, lower counter at the side for wheelchair users
Using a height-adjustable counter that the user can change themselves
questions.n: Equitable use focuses on providing the same means of use for all users to avoid stigmatization.

questions.q: In a vertical farming system (SDG 2), what is the primary architectural advantage of using 'Aeroponics' over 'Hydroponics' for high-rise buildings?
o: It significantly reduces the structural dead load of the building.
It allows the use of traditional soil to improve plant flavor.
It is easier to maintain without specialized plumbing.
It eliminates the need for artificial lighting.
questions.n: By misting roots instead of using heavy troughs of standing water, the overall weight on the building structure is much lower.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is most directly applied when an architect specifies 'D-shaped' cabinet pulls instead of small round knobs?
questions.n: D-shaped pulls can be used without a tight pinch grip, allowing users with arthritis or limited hand strength to operate them easily.

questions.q: Under SDG 12, 'Design for Disassembly' (DfD) is a strategy that supports a circular economy. What is a key architectural feature of DfD?
o: Using high-strength chemical adhesives for all joints
Using mechanical fasteners like bolts and screws instead of welds
Casting all plumbing and electrical lines directly into concrete slabs
questions.n: Mechanical connections allow components to be taken apart and reused without damaging the base materials.

questions.q: In an Aquaponics system (SDG 2), what happens if the 'Nitrifying Bacteria' are removed or die off?
o: The water will become clear and more oxygenated.
The plants will grow faster due to increased ammonia.
Ammonia levels will rise, eventually killing the fish.
The fish will begin to eat the plant roots.
questions.n: Without bacteria to convert ammonia into nitrates, the waste builds up to lethal levels for the aquatic life.

questions.q: Universal Design Principle 3, 'Simple and Intuitive Use,' suggests that architects should avoid 'unnecessary complexity.' Which of the following follows this rule?
o: An elevator panel that uses only Roman numerals for floor numbers
A restroom door with a lock that is cleverly hidden for aesthetic reasons
A standard fire exit push-bar (panic bar) that opens in the direction of egress
A high-tech touch screen that requires a multi-step login to open a public door
questions.n: The design is consistent with user expectations and requires no training or specialized knowledge to operate.

questions.q: Regarding SDG 6, what is the primary function of a 'Bioswale' in an urban parking lot design?
o: To provide a shaded area for cars
To store potable water for emergency use
To act as a noise barrier between the parking lot and the street
To filter and slow down stormwater runoff before it enters the municipal system
questions.n: Bioswales use vegetation and soil to capture pollutants and reduce the volume of peak runoff.

questions.q: Universal Design Principle 7, 'Size and Space for Approach and Use,' is most critical when designing which architectural element?
o: The volume of an emergency alarm
The turning radius inside a public restroom stall
The color contrast between a door and a wall
The font size on a room sign
questions.n: Principle 7 ensures that there is enough room for people of all sizes and those using mobility devices to maneuver comfortably.

questions.q: In tropical countries, which SDG 7-aligned passive cooling strategy involves a high-ceiling space with openings at the top to let hot air escape?
questions.n: Buoyancy-driven ventilation occurs when warm air rises and exits through high-level vents, drawing cooler air in at the bottom.

questions.q: Which of the following is a direct architectural application of SDG 3 (Good Health) through 'Indirect Nature' in Biophilic Design?
o: Designing a rooftop garden where employees can grow vegetables
Using organic patterns, wood-grain textures, and earth-tone colors in the interior
Providing an outdoor balcony for fresh air access
Installing a large window that overlooks a natural forest
questions.n: Indirect nature refers to evocations of nature through materials, patterns, and forms rather than the living things themselves.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is primarily addressed when an architect provides a 'braille' and 'high-contrast' sign for a public elevator?
questions.n: This principle ensures that necessary information is communicated effectively to the user, regardless of ambient conditions or the user's sensory abilities.

questions.q: In a high-density urban development targeting SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), what is the primary benefit of 'Hydroponics' over traditional soil-based rooftop gardens?
o: It uses more water to ensure plant health.
It requires less maintenance from mechanical systems.
It eliminates the need for any sunlight.
It allows for faster growth rates and higher yields in a smaller footprint.
questions.n: Direct nutrient delivery to the roots in a controlled environment accelerates plant growth and maximizes space efficiency.

questions.q: An architect specifies a ramp with a 1:12 slope and a wide landing at the top. Which Universal Design principle does this most directly support?
questions.n: A gentle slope and proper landing allow the user to navigate the level change with minimal fatigue and strain.

questions.q: Which 'Zero Hunger' (SDG 2) technique is characterized by suspending plants in a closed environment and misting the roots with a nutrient-rich solution?
questions.n: Aeroponics uses mist to nourish roots, requiring the least amount of water and no soil or liquid medium.

questions.q: If a building provides a power-operated sliding door alongside a manual swing door, which Universal Design principle is being demonstrated?
questions.n: Providing multiple ways to enter the building accommodates a wide range of individual preferences and abilities.

questions.q: In the context of SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption), what is the main goal of 'Design for Deconstruction'?
o: To minimize the initial cost of construction materials.
To ensure the building can be demolished quickly.
To use only biodegradable materials like wood.
To allow building components to be removed and reused in other projects without damage.
questions.n: This supports a circular economy by keeping materials in a high-value state rather than turning them into landfill.

questions.q: Which element of 'Aquaponics' (SDG 2) produces the waste that is eventually converted into fertilizer for the plants?
questions.n: Fish excrete ammonia as waste, which provides the primary nutrient base for the symbiotic system.

questions.q: An architect places a wide hallway with no obstacles and clear floor space for a 360-degree turn. Which Universal Design principle is being applied?
o: Size and Space for Approach and Use
questions.n: This principle ensures that appropriate size and space is provided for approach, reach, and maneuver regardless of user size or mobility.

questions.q: SDG 11 focuses on 'Sustainable Cities.' Which architectural practice contributes to this by reducing the 'Urban Heat Island' effect?
o: Reducing the amount of open public parks
Increasing the number of glass facades
Expanding the use of dark asphalt in parking lots
Using 'Cool Roofs' with high solar reflectance (Albedo)
questions.n: High albedo surfaces reflect sunlight rather than absorbing it, lowering local ambient temperatures.

questions.q: A lever-type door handle is preferred over a round knob in Universal Design. Which principle explains this?
questions.n: Levers can be operated with a closed fist or elbow, requiring less grip and torque than a knob.

questions.q: In terms of SDG 13 (Climate Action), what is the significance of 'Embodied Carbon' in materials like concrete and steel?
o: It represents the emissions from manufacturing, transport, and construction of the building.
It is the amount of carbon the building's trees can absorb.
It refers only to the waste generated at the construction site.
It is the carbon emitted during the operation of the building.
questions.n: Embodied carbon accounts for the total greenhouse gases emitted throughout a material's lifecycle from extraction to installation.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is applied when an elevator has a 'fail-safe' mechanism that prevents the doors from closing if an object is detected?
questions.n: This principle minimizes hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions.

questions.q: Urban agriculture using 'Vertical Farming' helps address SDG 2. What is a common architectural drawback of this system?
o: It makes the building structure more flexible.
It significantly increases the building's water and electrical demand.
questions.n: Pumping water and powering LED grow lights require significant energy compared to traditional outdoor farming.

questions.q: The use of 'Greywater' recycling for toilet flushing and landscape irrigation directly addresses which SDG?
questions.n: SDG 6 focuses on water efficiency and reducing the strain on freshwater supplies.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle requires that a design should be easy to understand, regardless of the user's language skills?
questions.n: This principle eliminates unnecessary complexity and uses universal icons or patterns that anyone can understand.

questions.q: In tropical architecture, a 'Solar Chimney' uses which principle to cool a building (SDG 7)?
questions.n: As air inside the chimney is heated by the sun, it rises and escapes out the top, drawing cooler air in from the bottom.

questions.q: Which of these is a violation of 'Equitable Use'?
o: A museum having a front entrance with stairs and a side entrance with a ramp.
A website that allows users to increase font size.
A building having an automatic sliding door for all visitors.
A park with a continuous paved path around a lake.
questions.n: This segregates users based on their ability, making the experience unequal and potentially stigmatizing.

questions.q: What is 'Aquaponics' a combination of?
questions.n: It combines fish farming (aquaculture) with soil-less plant growing (hydroponics) in a symbiotic cycle.

questions.q: Under SDG 11.7, which design strategy ensures that a public park is safe for women and vulnerable groups at night?
o: Reducing the number of lights to save energy
questions.n: Creating open vistas and well-lit paths makes a space feel safer because people can see and be seen.

questions.q: Which principle of Universal Design is being used when an architect provides both 'Visual' and 'Tactile' warnings at the edge of a subway platform?
questions.n: By providing redundancy (something you can see and something you can feel), the information reaches all users regardless of ability.

questions.q: What is the primary architectural goal of 'Adaptive Reuse' (SDG 11)?
o: To demolish old buildings to make room for new ones.
To build a modern building that looks old.
To restore a building exactly to its original historical state.
To repurpose an existing structure for a new function while preserving its heritage.
questions.n: This reduces the need for new materials (SDG 12) and preserves cultural history (SDG 11).

questions.q: In an Aeroponic system (SDG 2), how do the plants get their nutrients?
o: From being submerged in a fish tank
From chemical fertilizers in the ground
From a fine mist sprayed onto their roots
questions.n: The roots are suspended in the air and periodically sprayed with a nutrient-rich mist.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is most concerned with 'left-handed' vs. 'right-handed' users?
questions.n: This principle accommodates a wide range of individual preferences and abilities, including hand dominance.

questions.q: Why is 'Base Isolation' considered a part of SDG 9 (Infrastructure Resilience)?
o: It reduces the building's carbon footprint.
It is a cheaper way to build foundations.
It allows a building to withstand earthquakes by decoupling it from ground movement.
questions.n: Resilient infrastructure is key to SDG 9, ensuring buildings remain functional after a disaster.

questions.q: Which of these is the best example of 'Tolerance for Error' (Universal Design Principle 5)?
o: A hallway that is painted bright yellow.
A door with a very heavy handle.
An 'Undo' button on a digital control panel.
questions.n: It allows the user to reverse an accidental action without negative consequences.

questions.q: SDG 15 (Life on Land) encourages 'Green Infrastructure.' What is an example of this at the building scale?
o: A Green Roof or Living Wall
questions.n: These features provide habitats for birds/insects and help manage stormwater naturally.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is violated by a 'labyrinth' layout in a public hospital?
questions.n: A confusing layout requires high concentration and experience to navigate, violating Principle 3.

questions.q: What is 'Hydroponics'?
o: Growing plants in a nutrient-rich water solution without soil
Growing plants using only rain water
questions.n: This method uses water as the primary medium to deliver minerals to the roots.

questions.q: In the context of SDG 7, what is 'Passive Solar Heating'?
o: Using solar panels to heat water
Using a heat pump powered by the sun
Using south-facing windows and thermal mass to capture and store the sun's heat naturally
Painting a building black to absorb heat
questions.n: This architectural strategy requires no moving parts or electricity to function.

questions.q: Which of these is a hallmark of 'Biophilic Design' (SDG 3)?
o: Using only perfectly straight lines and sharp corners
Maximizing the use of concrete and steel
Designing completely windowless buildings to save energy
Integrating natural light, plants, and water features into the built environment
questions.n: This satisfies the human need to be connected to nature, improving mental and physical health.

questions.q: Under Universal Design Principle 2 (Flexibility in Use), an architect should provide 'choice' in methods of use. Which of these is an example?
o: A height-adjustable desk that works for a seated child or a standing adult
A heavy door that requires two hands to open
A sign with very small text
A standard height table for everyone
questions.n: This accommodates the physical preferences and sizes of a wide range of users.

questions.q: SDG 13 (Climate Action) encourages 'Net Zero Buildings.' What does this mean?
o: The building produces as much energy as it consumes over the course of a year.
The building cost zero dollars to build.
The building uses zero materials from nature.
questions.n: This is achieved through high efficiency and on-site renewable energy generation.

questions.q: Which of these food production methods uses the LEAST amount of water?
questions.n: By using a fine mist, aeroponics uses roughly 95% less water than traditional farming.

questions.q: Universal Design Principle 6 is 'Low Physical Effort.' Which architectural feature best represents this?
o: A heavy wooden door with a round knob
A touch-screen that requires precise finger taps
A staircase with very steep steps
questions.n: The user performs no physical action to start the water, minimizing effort and fatigue.

questions.q: Why is 'Urban Sprawl' considered a violation of SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities)?
o: Because it increases car dependency and destroys natural farmland.
Because it makes cities too quiet.
Because it makes public transport too efficient.
Because it encourages people to live in apartments.
questions.n: Sustainable cities should be 'compact' to reduce transport emissions and protect surrounding land.

questions.q: Which material has a LOWER 'Embodied Carbon' (SDG 13)?
questions.n: Trees sequester carbon while growing, and processing wood requires much less energy than melting steel or making cement.

questions.q: Universal Design Principle 1 is 'Equitable Use.' What is the key 'rule' for this principle?
o: The design should be very easy to read.
The means of use should be identical for all users whenever possible.
The design should have many different ways to be used.
questions.n: This ensures that no user is segregated, stigmatized, or treated as 'special' or 'different'.

questions.q: In 'Aquaponics,' what role do 'Nitrifying Bacteria' play?
o: They convert fish waste (ammonia) into plant food (nitrates).
They keep the water from freezing.
They provide food for the fish.
questions.n: Without these bacteria, the system would fail as ammonia would kill the fish and the plants would starve.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of 'Tolerance for Error' in a public park?
o: A park that is closed during the rain
A sharp metal edge on a bench
A bench with no back support
Rounded edges on all playground equipment and furniture
questions.n: This minimizes the consequences of an accidental fall or bump.

questions.q: SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption) promotes the 'Circular Economy.' How does an architect apply this?
o: By using as many new materials as possible.
By designing buildings that can be easily dismantled and their materials recycled.
By using materials that last forever and never change.
questions.n: This keeps materials in the 'loop' rather than ending up in a landfill.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is most helpful for someone who is 'distracted' or in a 'noisy' environment?
questions.n: When a design is intuitive, it requires low concentration, making it easy to use even when the user is stressed or distracted.

questions.q: In 'Vertical Farming' (SDG 2), what is 'LED Grow Lighting' used for?
o: To provide the specific light spectrum needed for photosynthesis indoors.
To make the building look modern at night.
questions.n: LEDs are efficient and can be tuned to the 'blue' and 'red' light plants need to grow.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is violated if a public kiosk only has 'audio' instructions and no screen or text?
questions.n: A kiosk must provide information in multiple modes (visual, tactile, audible) so everyone can perceive it.

questions.q: SDG 11 encourages 'Resilient' communities. What does 'Resilience' mean in architecture?
o: A building that has many people living in it.
The ability of a building or city to recover quickly from a disaster (flood, earthquake).
A building that is made of very expensive materials.
A building that never needs maintenance.
questions.n: Resilience is about 'bouncing back' and maintaining function after a shock.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle ensures that there is enough room for a service animal or an assistant to accompany a user?
o: Size and Space for Approach and Use
questions.n: This principle requires that space be provided for 'assistance or assistive devices' as well as the user.

questions.q: In 'Hydroponics,' what is 'Rockwool' or 'Perlite' used for?
o: As a growing medium to physically support the plant's roots.
questions.n: They provide structure for the roots to hold onto while the water delivers the food.

questions.q: Which Universal Design principle is most directly applied when a kitchen has 'pull-out' shelves instead of deep fixed ones?
questions.n: Pull-out shelves allow the user to see and reach items without bending or reaching deep, minimizing strain.

questions.q: What is 'Biomimicry' in the context of SDG 9?
o: Destroying nature to build something better.
Using only natural materials like mud.
Designing materials or systems that copy nature's functional processes (e.g., self-cleaning glass like a lotus leaf).
Building a house that looks like a tree.
questions.n: This leads to highly efficient and sustainable innovations.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'Social' benefit of SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities)?
o: Lower energy bills for the city council.
Increased social interaction through walkable neighborhoods and public plazas.
questions.n: Walkable cities foster 'community' and reduce the isolation of car-based sprawl.

questions.q: Universal Design Principle 5 (Tolerance for Error) suggests providing 'Warnings' for hazards. What is the most effective way to do this?
o: A tiny sign that is hard to see.
No warning at all to avoid scaring people.
A sign that is written in only one language.
A multi-sensory warning (e.g., a beep AND a flashing light).
questions.n: This ensures that the warning is received even if the user is distracted or has a sensory impairment.
